text.headline: Social Insects Emerge
text.text: Eusocial insects (ants, bees, termites) develop kin-based cooperation. Workers sacrifice reproduction to help relatives, demonstrating the earliest forms of cooperative behavior driven by genetic relatedness.

events.notes: Examples: Ants share food through trophallaxis; bees perform waggle dances to share resource locations. Hamilton's rule (1964) explains this as kin selection.

text.headline: Reciprocal Grooming in Mammals
text.text: Early mammals develop reciprocal grooming behaviors, exchanging hygiene services in ways that require tracking social relationships and remembering past interactions.

events.notes: Examples: Vampire bats share blood meals with roost-mates who groomed them. Grooming relationships in mammals correlate with coalition support during conflicts.

text.headline: Primate Coalition Formation
text.text: Primate ancestors begin forming coalitions for mutual defense and resource access. This requires sophisticated social cognition to track alliances, enemies, and past exchanges.

events.notes: Examples: Baboons form male-male alliances; female macaques support relatives in conflicts. Coalition formation requires memory of who helped whom.

text.headline: Inequity Aversion Emerges
text.text: Old World monkeys demonstrate inequity aversion—negative reactions to receiving less than a partner for the same work. This suggests emotional responses to unfair treatment.

events.notes: Research: Brosnan & de Waal (2003) showed capuchins reject cucumber when partners receive grapes. Similar responses found in chimpanzees, dogs, and corvids.

text.headline: Complex Social Tracking
text.text: Hominid ancestors develop sophisticated abilities to track multiple social relationships, remember past exchanges, and anticipate future interactions—cognitive prerequisites for fairness norms.

events.notes: The 'social brain hypothesis' links primate brain size to social group complexity. Tracking fairness in large groups requires substantial cognitive resources.

text.headline: Punishment of Free-Riders
text.text: Early humans show evidence of third-party punishment—sanctioning cheaters even at personal cost. This enforcement mechanism stabilizes cooperation in larger groups.

events.notes: Archaeological evidence suggests communal hunting required fair sharing. Groups with punishment mechanisms outcompeted those without, selecting for fairness enforcement.

text.headline: Explicit Fairness Norms
text.text: Homo sapiens develops language-mediated fairness norms—explicit rules about sharing, reciprocity, and justice that can be taught across generations and applied to novel situations.

events.notes: Language enables abstract fairness principles beyond specific situations. Cultural transmission allows fairness norms to accumulate and become more sophisticated over time.

text.headline: Cross-Cultural Universals Documented
text.text: Research using economic games (Ultimatum, Dictator, Public Goods) documents fairness concerns across all human cultures studied, though specific norms vary with economic systems and social organization.

events.notes: Henrich et al. (2010) found fairness in 15 small-scale societies worldwide. All cultures show some fairness concern, but 'fair' offers range from 25-50% depending on cultural context.
